title: Heap index math + sift skeleton
description: The whiteboard boilerplate for a 0-indexed array heap: parent/child index math plus sift-up and sift-down loops.

notes: A heap is just an array — no node objects. The tree shape is encoded by the index math.
Parent = (i-1) >> 1, left = 2*i+1, right = 2*i+2 — memorize these three formulas.
Sift UP after a push (new item is at the tail). Sift DOWN after a pop-root (move last to index 0, then bubble down).
On sift-down ALWAYS swap with the smaller child — swapping with the larger would leave the smaller child violating the heap property.

questions.q: For a 0-indexed array heap, the parent of index 7 is:
The left child of index 3 sits at which index?
Why is a heap implemented over an array instead of with node objects?
options: Arrays are faster to iterate in JS
Index math (parent/left/right) encodes the tree shape compactly with no pointers
Node objects can't hold numbers
Arrays auto-sort their contents
questions.explain: The complete binary tree shape maps perfectly onto contiguous array indices — no parent/child pointers needed.

questions.q: When do you sift UP vs sift DOWN?
options: Sift up on insert (bubble from the tail); sift down on pop-root (bubble from index 0)
Sift down on insert; sift up on pop-root
Sift up for both
Sift down for both
questions.explain: Insert appends at the tail then sifts up. Pop-root swaps root with the tail, shrinks, then sifts down from index 0.

questions.q: On a MIN-heap sift-DOWN, you swap the node with the LARGER of its two children. What breaks?
options: Nothing — either child works
The smaller child stays below a larger value, violating the heap property at that subtree
It becomes a max-heap
The array length changes
questions.explain: Promoting the larger child leaves the smaller child sitting under a bigger parent — the min-heap invariant (parent ≤ both children) is violated. Always swap with the SMALLER child.

questions.q: Building a heap by `heapify` (sift-down from the bottom up) over n elements is:
options: O(n log n) — n inserts each O(log n)
O(n) — most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a few levels
O(n²)
O(log n)
questions.explain: Bottom-up heapify is O(n): half the nodes are leaves (0 work), a quarter sift at most 1 level, etc. — the weighted sum converges to O(n), unlike n separate O(log n) inserts.

questions.q: To turn the min-heap code into a MAX-heap, what's the minimal change?
options: Swap the parent/child index formulas
Flip the comparisons (use `>` where it used `<`) so larger values bubble toward the root
Reverse the array first
Use sift-up only, never sift-down
questions.explain: The index math is identical; only the ordering comparisons flip — a max-heap keeps the largest at the root by reversing every `<`/`>` in the sift logic.

questions.q: You need repeated 'give me the current min, then add more items' on a changing dataset. Why a heap over a sorted array?
options: A heap keeps everything fully sorted, which a sorted array can't
Insert is O(log n) on a heap vs O(n) to keep a sorted array sorted; you only pay for the min you actually extract
A sorted array can't return the minimum
Heaps use less memory than arrays
questions.explain: A heap gives O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min without maintaining a total order; inserting into a sorted array to stay sorted is O(n) per insert.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the parent/left/right index math for a 0-indexed array heap.

blanks.hint: bit-shift right by 1 — integer-halves a non-negative int

exercises.prompt: Fill in the sift-up skeleton: swap with the parent while the parent is larger, then move i up.

blanks.hint: destination of the swap is the parent slot
ES swap idiom — RHS is [parent, child]
after the swap, the new item now lives at index p — keep bubbling from there

L3.prompt: Given the min-heap array [1, 5, 3, 10, 8, 7], use the parent index formula to find the parent of position 4, then log the value stored at that parent index.
hints: parent(4) = 1, and heap[1] is the second element.
